1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4.name: Italian Game
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4.background: Developed in the sixteenth century by players such as Pedro Damiano and Giulio Polerio, it features prominently in the game collections of Gioachino Greco from the 1620s. The name Italian Game was not common in English until the late twentieth century.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6.background: First recorded by Giulio Cesare Polerio around 1580. Also known as the Prussian Defence, its theory was developed extensively in the 19th century.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and hits e4 in one move, the more combative of the two main replies. The price is that the knight blocks the queen's control of g5, so Black must be ready for an attack on f7 and has to know the theory; in return Black gets active counterplay.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5.strategy: Mirrors White's bishop and keeps the queen's control of g5, so there is no sudden attack on f7. A slower, more positional choice than the sharp alternative, in which the fight is over the d4 square and which side builds the centre first.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7.name: Italian Game: Hungarian Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7.background: Named after a correspondence game between Paris and Pest, Hungary, played from 1842 to 1845; Carlo Cozio had already analysed the move in the 18th century.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7.strategy: A cautious reply that avoids the sharp lines and keeps the position solid, but does little to challenge White's centre. Black accepts a slightly cramped game: White has more space and freer development, and Black plays mostly for safety.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 h6.name: Italian Game: Anti-Fried Liver Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 h6.strategy: Takes g5 away from White's knight in advance, so that ...Nf6 can follow without allowing an attack on f7. The cost is a move spent on a pawn, which gives White time for a strike in the centre. A sound but slow precaution.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 d6.name: Italian Game: Paris Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 d6.background: 3...d6, also called the Semi-Italian Opening, was popular in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries but is rarely seen today.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn and keeps the position solid, an old-fashioned set-up. It restricts the king's bishop and leaves White the space and the choice of plan, but there is little to refute.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nd4.name: Italian Game: Blackburne-Kostić Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nd4.background: Wilhelm Steinitz made the first known mention of the line in 1895, in the addenda to his Modern Chess Instructor, and Borislav Kostić played it in the early twentieth century. Blackburne reputedly won a shilling a game with its trap, though no games of his with it are recorded.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nd4.strategy: Moves the same knight again and offers the e5 pawn as bait: after the greedy capture on e5, ...Qg5 attacks the knight and g2, and a further grab on f7 walks into a smothered mate. If White simply trades on d4, Black has wasted time and stands worse.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 f5.name: Italian Game: Rousseau Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 f5.background: Named after the French master Eugène Rousseau; it is also called the Ponziani Countergambit, after Domenico Lorenzo Ponziani.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 f5.strategy: A counter-gambit that weakens Black's own king: the c4 bishop already looks straight at g8, which makes castling short awkward, and the e8-h5 diagonal is open. White meets it by striking in the centre and keeps a clear edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.d4.strategy: Claims the centre at once while Black's bishop on e7 does not bear on d4 as it would from c5. If Black takes, White recaptures with the knight and has more space and the freer development, so Black must be ready for a cramped, defensive game, the price of this solid set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.d3.strategy: Keeps the centre closed and develops without committing. White gives up the immediate grab for space but avoids early exchanges and aims for a slow manoeuvring game, in which Black's solid set-up is not under pressure.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.O-O.strategy: Castles first and leaves the centre to a later decision. It is passive: Black has time to complete a solid set-up, so White gives up the space advantage that taking the centre at once would claim.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.c3.strategy: Prepares to occupy the centre with a pawn behind it, but it is slower than playing d4 at once and takes the natural c3 square from the knight. Black develops with a threat against e4, so White ends up without the space advantage of the main line.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.d4 exd4.name: Scotch Game: Benima Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Resolves the tension by taking, so White must recapture or sacrifice. After the usual recapture with the knight White has more space and the freer pieces, and Black has to be content with a solid but slightly cramped position, a safe way to play for equality rather than for the advantage.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.d4 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn rather than trading on d4, so the tension stays and White decides the structure. Black keeps a compact, flexible position, but White can simplify, gain space or keep the tension and the freer piece play, each with a slight edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.d4 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4 but ignores the tension in the centre: White takes on e5 with tempo on the knight. The natural grab on e4 then runs into Qd5, which attacks the knight and f7 together, so Black has to retreat and give up the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Offers a second pawn for development instead of simply recapturing: if Black grabs it with ...dxc3, Qd5 puts heavy pressure on f7. Black can decline by developing, though, so the gambit is weaker than the plain recapture on d4, which keeps more space.

Recaptures the pawn at once and puts the knight on a strong central square with an attack on the c6-knight. Material is level and White has more space and the freer pieces, while Black, with the bishop already on e7, is left a little cramped.

Castles and leaves the pawn on d4 in Black's hands in return for a lead in development. White can win it back later, but Black can hold it by developing, so the gambit gives White less than the plain recapture, which keeps more space.

Develops with an attack on the e4-pawn, which nothing defends, and keeps the extra pawn on d4. White must answer at once, and the push that does it gives White space and the initiative; Black is a pawn up, but White has the more comfortable game.

Attacks the c4-bishop at once instead of taking a second pawn. White has to give up the bishop for the knight by taking on d4 with the queen, or sacrifice a pawn, so Black gets the bishop pair and a solid, healthy position.

Takes a second pawn and opens the game: Qd5 aims queen and bishop at f7, where only the king stands guard, so Black must defend with care while White's lead in development gets time to work. Playable, but riskier than hitting the bishop at once.

Drives the knight away with a pawn that gains space. The extra pawn on d4, attacked three times, will be won back, and White comes out with the better development and central space in return for an advanced e-pawn that Black can try to attack.

Castles and offers the e4 pawn instead of forcing matters. If Black takes it, White recovers the d4 pawn but stays a pawn down and has to prove compensation in the centre; a rare gambit that gives Black an easy choice.

Retakes at once and leaves e4 loose: Black can win a second pawn, but White's open lines and lead in development give enough play in return. A sound gambit, but the e-pawn advance gets its play without giving anything away.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Hungarian Defence, Tartakower Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Centralises the knight, which hits c3 and f2, rather than retreating it. Black keeps the extra pawn for the moment; the knight is exposed to attack and White's space advantage tells, so Black must defend with care, but this is the most active way to meet the pawn.
Hits e5 a second time and eyes f2, but the knight stands on the rim and cxd4 shores up e5 for good. White has the pawn back and the better centre, and Black's extra pawn is gone.
Hangs the knight: Bxd5 takes it and Black cannot recapture, since the d7 pawn blocks the queen's way to d5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Modern Bishop's Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3.background: Sometimes called the Modern Bishop's Opening, because it is commonly reached from the Bishop's Opening by 2.Bc4 Nf6 3.d3 Nc6 4.Nf3. It became popular in the 1980s and has been used by John Nunn and others.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: The solid main line: a pawn defends e4 and the c1-bishop's diagonal opens, and White avoids the early tactics of the sharper fourth moves. White builds the centre slowly, aiming for a manoeuvring game and a central break once the pieces are ready.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Open Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once and offers a pawn for development: if Black takes, White plays for the initiative with open lines towards f7. A sharp, open game in which Black has to keep an eye on the king and cannot afford loose play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5.strategy: Piles up on f7 with knight and bishop before the rest of the army is out, forcing Black to sacrifice a pawn or take wild risks. It is the sharpest test of the Two Knights: Black equalises with accurate play, but a player who misses the point loses quickly.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3.name: Four Knights Game: Italian Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3.background: Popular in the 1880s, though some authors regard it as inferior; Nigel Short used it successfully against Antoaneta Stefanova in 2003.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move, but it allows the fork trick: Black takes on e4 and, after the recapture, plays ...d5 to hit bishop and knight at once, reaching an easy, level game. Sound but second-rate, since White has handed Black a simple route to equality.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.O-O.strategy: Castles and offers the e4-pawn for an open game and quick development. If Black takes it, White gets active pieces and open lines and the game stays level, but there is no need to give a pawn when sound development is on offer. A playable gambit, not a main line.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 Bc5.strategy: Puts the bishop on its most active diagonal, aimed at f2, and reaches the quiet position that 3...Bc5 4.d3 Nf6 produces. Both sides build slowly: White prepares a central break and Black's well-placed pieces keep the answer to it ready, a long fight for the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 Be7.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Modern Bishop's Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 Be7.strategy: A solid, modest set-up: the bishop stays behind the pawns and gives up the active diagonal against f2. Black is a little passive but safe, in a slow manoeuvring game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 h6.strategy: Takes the g5 square from White's bishop and knight, so there is no pin on the f6-knight and no pressure on f7 from g5, and it may prepare a kingside pawn advance later. It costs a tempo in development: playable, but slow.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 h6 5.O-.strategy: Finishes the kingside development and keeps every central plan open; with the game still quiet there is no hurry to commit. The king now stands on the wing where Black's h6 pawn may support a later advance, so White has to watch that plan.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 h6 5.c3.strategy: Prepares the central break d4 with a pawn behind it and gives the c4-bishop the b3 and c2 retreat squares, the plan of a slow, manoeuvring game. Black's h6 is a modest waiting move, so White can build at leisure and open the centre when the pieces are placed.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 h6 5.Nc.strategy: Develops the knight to a natural square where it guards e4 and eyes d5 and b5. White chooses piece play over a pawn centre, a symmetrical, manoeuvring game in which White does little to exploit Black's h6.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 h6 5.O-.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Modern Bishop's Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 h6 5.O-.strategy: Shores up e5 with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal, completing a compact set-up in which the h6 pawn already denies White's pieces the g5 square. Black stays flexible and solid, and the game is a slow fight where neither side has an easy break.

Develops the bishop to its most active diagonal, eyeing f2, and keeps the d-pawn flexible. With h6 already denying the g5 square, the knight on f6 cannot be pinned, so Black can settle for a slow, balanced game of manoeuvring and wait for White to commit.

Develops the bishop to a safe square and prepares to castle, backing up the knight on f6. It is solid but passive: it puts no pressure on White's position, so Black reacts while White decides how the centre is built.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4.name: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Dubois Réti Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the offered pawn: the e4-pawn is now attacked by the knight and nothing defends it, so White has to push the pawn or sacrifice it for development. Black has the extra pawn and the central tension is gone, but must defend against White's quick play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 d6.name: Italian Game: Scotch Invitation Declined
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 d6.strategy: Defends e5 without releasing the tension, declining the gambit. It keeps Black solid but passive: White can simplify by trading queens into a drawish game, or gain space by pushing the d-pawn at the c6-knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 Bd6.strategy: Defends e5 a second time with the bishop and keeps the tension in the centre, but the bishop stands in front of the d-pawn and on a square the e-pawn can attack. Once White has castled and Black takes on d4, e5 hits bishop and knight together and White gets the slightly better game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Advance Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..background: Often adopted by Evgeny Sveshnikov, this line has gradually become the main line of the Open Variation.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: The modern way to play the gambit: the pawn gains space and drives the knight away, so White is not forced to give up e4. Black keeps the extra pawn on d4 for now, but has to spend time on the knight while White's pieces come out with tempo.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: The traditional gambit: White castles and lets Black take e4 for development and pressure down the open e-file. Black's best reply, taking the pawn, gives material back for a level game, so this is sound but offers White little more than equality.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence, Perreux Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: A tricky second attack on f7 while the pawn still stands on d4. It moves a piece twice and leaves e4 undefended, and Black's counter in the centre forces White to give up castling and to defend, so White is the one who has to be careful.

Hits the c4-bishop with a pawn, so White cannot simply regain the pawn on d4 and has to find a good square for the bishop, while the e5-pawn still attacks the knight. The most natural and common answer: Black keeps the extra pawn and fights for the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Scotch Game: Scotch Gambit, Kingside Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Steps away from the pawn and hits e5 a second time, with the knight on g4 as well as the one on c6, while eyeing f2. The knight is far from home and f7 is left to the king alone, so it is playable but rarely best; White has to defend e5 and then use the tempo.

Jumps to the central square beyond the e5 pawn's reach and keeps the extra pawn for now. Black has to support the knight and challenge the c4-bishop soon, while White castles and builds pressure on the centre; the game is open and about level.

Steps out of the pawn's attack with a pin: the c6-knight, the only piece guarding d4, cannot move without exposing the king, so White threatens to win the pawn back at once with Nxd4. The main line leads to a sharp, balanced fight with active play for both sides.

Takes the attacked knight, but ...dxc4 takes the bishop in return, and the advanced pawn is soon lost again: White is at least a pawn down, with only the open e-file to show for it, while Black's d4 and c4 pawns cramp it.

Retreats out of the d5 pawn's reach but gives up the pin on the c6-knight, the point of the main line. White can regain the d4 pawn only by trading knights, while Black's knight finds a good square in the centre and Black keeps the more comfortable game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, Max Lange Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Puts the knight on the central e4 square, where the d5 pawn supports it and the e5 pawn cannot reach it. Black lets White regain the d4 pawn in exchange for a firm centre and active pieces, and the pin on the c6-knight has to be resolved; the position is sharp but balanced.
Unpins the c6-knight but leaves the knight on f6 attacked by the e5 pawn: White takes on c6 first and then on f6, and comes out a piece up for the pawns.

Steps away from the e5 pawn and attacks it, but the c6-knight is pinned and cannot help: White simply takes back on d4, since the pinned knight cannot recapture, and the knight on g4 is left far from the other pieces.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, Double Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: The best reply: Black takes the second pawn and the centre pawns White offered are gone. White's compensation is development and the open e-file, but Black gives material back to settle the position and reaches a comfortable, level game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, Janowski Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Builds a pawn wall and opens the c8-bishop instead of grabbing e4, but it leaves the d4-pawn to be won back at once and gives White the freer pieces. Solid but second-rate: Black has not made use of the extra pawn.

Develops the bishop to its most active square, defends the extra pawn on d4 and aims at f2. It invites the sharp e5 that White is hoping for and reaches a heavily analysed attack by transposition, so Black is theoretically fine but has to walk a narrow path.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, de Riviere Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: A modest developing move that prepares to castle and leaves the d4-pawn to White's recapture. Black stays solid and safe but passive, and hands White the freer development.

Pins the undefended knight on e4 to the king, so Black must block the file at once or lose it. White is two pawns down for the moment, but has the lead in development and open lines in return, and the pawns are soon won back.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Italian Game: Scotch Gambit, Nakhmanson Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: A gambit on a gambit: the knight attacks the one on e4 and offers a piece for an attack on the king if Black takes it. But Black can simply exchange knights and, with the better structure after the recapture on c3, gets the more comfortable game.

Regains a pawn at once by taking on d4, and after the exchange of knights the queen attacks the e4-knight. But it gives up the pin that Re1 sets, and with it the compensation: Black keeps a healthy extra pawn and has time to develop.
Blocks the pin with a pawn that also attacks the c4-bishop. White regains the material, but Black gives back the extra pawn for a safe king and a comfortable, level position.
Defends the pinned knight with a pawn, but one defender is not enough: Nc3 adds a second attacker, and after the exchanges on e4 the open e-file points at Black's king in the centre.

Does not break the pin, only changes its target: the e4-knight is now pinned to the queen and cannot move without losing it, so White can pile on it with Nxd4 and Qxd4 while Black's pieces are still at home.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nxe4.strategy: Grabs the pawn with a knight that White can take, and that is the idea: after the recapture ...d5 forks bishop and knight, so Black regains the piece with a good game. The sacrifice is only temporary, and it is why this fourth move is judged inferior.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop to the diagonal aimed at f2 and settles for a normal, balanced game in which both sides develop their pieces. Black passes up the chance to equalise by force with the knight capture and to put White on the defensive, but nothing is wrong with the move.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop to a safe square and prepares to castle, keeping everything protected. It is solid but passive, because the bishop pressures nothing, and it passes up the chance to put White on the defensive with the knight capture.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nxe4 5.strategy: The natural recapture and the main line: White wins the pawn back. Black's reply ...d5 forks bishop and knight, but after the exchanges material is level, so White gets a quiet, equal game and Black the easier play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nxe4 5.name: Four Knights Game: Italian Variation, Noa Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nxe4 5.strategy: Gives the bishop for a pawn to drag the king out, but after Kxf7 and the recapture on e4 the attack runs out of steam. White has lost the bishop pair and the centre to Black, whose king is safe and whose pawns are strong.

A pawn gambit: White castles at once and lets Black keep the e4 pawn, hoping for quick development and play against the king. Black can simply trade knights and keep the extra pawn, so the gambit asks more of White than it gives.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nxe4 5.name: Italian Game: Two Knights Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Nc3 Nxe4 5.strategy: The fork trick: the pawn attacks both the bishop and the knight, so White cannot keep both, but after the exchanges material comes out level. Black has equalised easily.
Defends e5 but misses the fork: with the pawn still on d7, neither the knight on e4 nor the bishop on c4 is attacked, and Black is a knight down for a pawn with nothing to show for it.
Develops the bishop with an eye on f2, but the knight on e4 simply takes it: Black has already given a knight for a pawn, and this loses a second piece for nothing.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.O-O Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop to its most active square, where it eyes f2 and discourages White's central break, since a pawn on d4 can be taken. Black declines the sharp pawn grab on e4 and keeps a flexible, natural position.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.O-O Nxe4.strategy: Grabs the pawn that castling left undefended, leaving Black a pawn up. White's compensation is a lead in development and pressure on the e-file against the knight, so Black must support the knight and finish developing carefully before the extra pawn counts.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.O-O Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop to a safe square and prepares castling without grabbing the pawn or choosing an active diagonal. Black gets a calm, equal game, but the bishop is less active than on c5 and White has time to build the centre.
